title: All companions gone
hookLine: every companion left, none stayed to the end; only the Lord remains (Salok M9 55, ang 1429)
last: STRENGTH RETURNED — ALL IS IN YOUR HANDS.

cards: Hospital waiting rooms tell the truth about friendship. At the wedding there were two hundred people. At the birthday, the house was full.
Then someone gets a long illness, and by the third month the visitors thin out. Nobody means it. People get busy; they don't know what to say; they assume someone else is going.
And the patient notices, quietly, who is still coming on Tuesday afternoons. Guru Tegh Bahadur has a stark two-line salok about that thinning out. And the story around it holds a surprise.

teach.h: SANG SAKHAA: ALL MY COMPANIONS LEFT.
teach.b: Salok fifty-five, Ang fourteen twenty-nine. In paraphrase: all my companions and friends have left me; no one kept company with me to the end. Nanak says, in this calamity, my one support is the Lord.
Sang sakhaa: companions, friends. Sabh taj gae: all have gone.
Kou na nibhio saath: no one saw the companionship through. Nibhaana is a rich Punjabi verb: to keep something going to the end, a promise, a friendship, faith when it costs.

teach.h: THE ONE PROP IN THE DISASTER.
teach.b: Then the second line: in this bipat, this disaster, the one tek, the one prop, is the Lord. The salok uses the name Raghunaath, a name for God that Gurbani borrows from the old stories of Rama.
It continues the run we've been reading: Rama gone, nothing stays, strength gone. Now the people go too, and what remains is God. Here is the surprise.
Sikh tradition remembers that when Guru Tegh Bahadur was held in Delhi, three Sikhs did stay with him: Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das, and Bhai Dayala.
Tradition says they were executed in front of him, before his own death, and Sikhs remember them by name to this day.
So the salok describes the way of the world, and the story honors the rare people who refused to be the way of the world. It names where the salok finds the final support.
And it quietly asks: when someone you love is in the bipat, will you be the one who nibhaaes, who sees it through?

how: Salok fifty-five is read among the closing saloks of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs remember Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das and Bhai Dayala, who stayed with Guru Tegh Bahadur in Delhi.

o: a vow to stay beside a friend in trouble
a short prayer said before a long journey
a prop, the one support when everyone else goes

games.q: all companions gone — tap the pairs.

s: Sikh tradition says no one at all stayed with Guru Tegh Bahadur in Delhi
tradition remembers three who stayed: Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das and Bhai Dayala.
Raghunaath is a name for God that Gurbani borrows from the Rama stories
the salok calls the Lord Raghunaath, the one support.
nibhaana means keeping something going to the end
no one nibhaaed, no one saw the companionship through.

games.q: a friend's long illness is in its third month and the visitors have thinned out. you're busy too. what does the story around salok fifty-five honor?
o: sending a card and moving on.
being the one who stays to the end.
games.why: the salok names the world's way, and Sikhs honor the three who refused it and stayed with the Guru in Delhi.

practice: Remember a time someone stayed with you through something hard, who kept calling, who kept showing up, and thank them silently.

Then think of someone in a long hard stretch now, an illness, a grief, a lonely year, and picture yourself as the Tuesday afternoon visitor, not the crowd at the wedding: a call, a meal dropped off, ten minutes sitting with them.
If you pray, hold them before God and say Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Tek, a prop, a support. Sang sakhaa sabh taj gae: everyone left, and in the bipat, the one tek is the Lord.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: tek, a prop or support; salok fifty-five calls the Lord the one tek in the calamity.

carryVoice: Your line: he remains. And now and then, so does a friend who sees it through. Day six hundred six.
